setup: I've finally started getting eight hours of sleep a night.
punchline: Spread across the week.
targetAssumption: Eight hours every night. It sounds like a self-improvement brag.
reinterpretation: The eight hours are a weekly total, so they're sleeping about an hour a night.
whyItWorks: The number stays true and only the unit changes. Three short words in the punch, ending on the word that flips it.

setup: Take my wife.
punchline: Please.
targetAssumption: "Take my wife" means "for example, my wife", and a story is coming.
reinterpretation: "Take" as in "take her away", as a request.
whyItWorks: Henny Youngman's famous four-word joke is the purest connector ever written: one ambiguous verb, one word to flip it. The pause before "Please" does half the work.

setup: My CV lists three skills:
punchline: Excel, PowerPoint and crying quietly in the stairwell.
targetAssumption: A list of office software skills.
reinterpretation: The third "skill" is a coping mechanism, which is also, honestly, a skill.
whyItWorks: Two real skills set the pattern. The third breaks it but is still technically true, and the specific location (stairwell) makes it a picture rather than a concept.

setup: My phone is so old,
punchline: its software updates come by post.
targetAssumption: A complaint about something slow: lag, battery.
reinterpretation: So old it belongs to a pre-internet world where updates arrive in an envelope.
whyItWorks: Classic "so X that Y" structure, but the exaggeration lives in the consequence, not the adjective. "Post" is a picture from a different era.

setup: Flat-pack furniture is like dating.
punchline: The pictures lie and there's always a spare screw.
targetAssumption: A tenuous comparison that'll need explaining.
reinterpretation: Two details that are true of both: misleading photos and something unaccounted for at the end.
whyItWorks: The proof is two-for-two. Each detail works literally for furniture and figuratively for dating, so the audience gets to complete the double meaning themselves.

setup: My boss told me to go the extra mile.
punchline: So I did. I'm emailing you from the motorway.
targetAssumption: "Go the extra mile" means put in more effort.
reinterpretation: An actual mile, travelled, while still technically working.
whyItWorks: Corporate idioms are fertile ground because everyone hates them. "So I did" signals obedience, and the location proves it.

setup: I sang at karaoke last night and got a standing ovation.
punchline: Everyone stood up to leave.
targetAssumption: Standing means applause. The singer was great.
reinterpretation: They were standing because they were going.
whyItWorks: The setup is a brag and the punch is a humiliation, built from the same physical action.

setup: My dad warned me that phones would rot my brain.
punchline: He now has four Facebook accounts and a feud with a bakery.
targetAssumption: The wise parent was right, or at least immune.
reinterpretation: The person giving the warning is the worst affected.
whyItWorks: Role reversal plus specificity. "A feud with a bakery" is so oddly precise it feels true, and "bakery" lands last.

setup: If my cat wrote my performance review:
punchline: "Meets expectations at opening tins. Needs improvement at being home."
targetAssumption: A cat's opinion would be about cat things.
reinterpretation: The cat uses HR's exact phrases to judge you as staff.
whyItWorks: The jargon of world two ("meets expectations", "needs improvement") is applied straight-faced to world one. Ending on "being home" adds a sneaky, sad truth.

setup: Self-checkouts are stupid. I scan my own shopping, I bag my own shopping,
punchline: and then a guard checks I didn't rob myself.
targetAssumption: A list of chores the shop has outsourced to you.
reinterpretation: If you're the cashier, the only person you could rob is yourself.
whyItWorks: The attitude (stupid) is stated up front, then proven with a rhythm of three. The third beat exposes the absurd logic.

setup: I'm in the best shape of my life.
punchline: Admittedly, that shape is a pear.
targetAssumption: "Shape" means fitness.
reinterpretation: "Shape" as a literal geometric shape.
whyItWorks: Self-deprecation lands well for new comics: the audience relaxes when you're the target. The fruit makes it a cheerful image rather than a sad one.

setup: Every family holiday has three stages:
punchline: excitement, packing and the silent treatment.
targetAssumption: The stages of a trip in order: plan, pack, go.
reinterpretation: The third stage is emotional, and it's the one everyone actually remembers.
whyItWorks: A recognisable truth in list form. The third item is slightly longer, which gives it a rhythmic weight.

setup: My mum's lasagne is so dense,
punchline: NASA has asked to study its gravity.
targetAssumption: It's heavy, filling, sits in your stomach.
reinterpretation: Dense as in astrophysics: it has its own gravitational field.
whyItWorks: "Dense" bridges cooking and physics. Bringing in a real institution (NASA) makes the absurd sound official.

setup: Reading the comments section is like eating petrol-station sushi.
punchline: You know exactly how it ends, and you still go back for seconds.
targetAssumption: Comments are bad. That's the point being made.
reinterpretation: The joke is on the reader: the comparison shows the compulsion, not just the quality.
whyItWorks: The comparison is the setup and the shared behaviour is the punch. "Seconds" is both a food word and the reveal of self-sabotage.

setup: My dad says he's between jobs.
punchline: Since March, he's been between the sofa cushions.
targetAssumption: "Between jobs" is a polite way of saying unemployed, temporarily.
reinterpretation: Physically between: sunk into the sofa.
whyItWorks: The time detail is moved to the front of the punch so the image ("cushions") comes last. Compare it with "…cushions since March", which ends on a date and fizzles.

setup: I put a lock on the biscuit tin to stop the kids. They learned to pick it in a day.
punchline: I'm still on the YouTube tutorial.
targetAssumption: The parent is in control and the lock works.
reinterpretation: The parent is now the one trying to break in.
whyItWorks: Two flips. The kids beat the lock, then the parent becomes the burglar of their own tin, and is worse at it than the kids.

setup: Our meeting was so pointless,
punchline: the minutes just said how many minutes.
targetAssumption: "The minutes" are the meeting notes, listing decisions.
reinterpretation: Minutes of time: the only fact worth recording is how long it took.
whyItWorks: The same word is used twice with two meanings, and ending on the second one makes the switch audible.

setup: A wedding is basically a hostage situation with a buffet.
punchline: Nobody can leave, everyone's smiling for the cameras, and an uncle is making demands.
targetAssumption: The hostage line is the whole joke.
reinterpretation: Every hostage-movie detail fits a real wedding.
whyItWorks: The mash-up is declared in the setup and proven by a rule of three in the punch. Each item is true of both worlds, and the third (the uncle) is the most recognisable.

setup: The scariest sentence at work is "Can I borrow you for a sec?"
punchline: Nobody has ever been returned.
targetAssumption: "Borrow you" is a harmless figure of speech.
reinterpretation: If you're borrowed, you should be returned, and nobody ever is.
whyItWorks: The attitude (scary) frames it, and the punch takes "borrow" literally to prove it. Short punch, final word does everything.

setup: Being an adult is hard.
punchline: Nobody gives you a sticker for eating a vegetable.
targetAssumption: Adult life is hard because of bills and work.
reinterpretation: It's hard because nobody rewards the tiny wins anymore.
whyItWorks: Attitude (hard) plus a childlike detail. The gap between the serious claim and the small proof is the laugh.

setup: My teenager sleeps in so late,
punchline: the neighbours think he's a rumour.
targetAssumption: He sleeps until noon.
reinterpretation: So late that, to the outside world, he doesn't exist.
whyItWorks: Exaggerates the social consequence rather than the time. "Rumour" is an unexpected, precise word.

setup: Having a teenager is like owning a cat.
punchline: Ignored all day, needed at midnight, thanked never.
targetAssumption: A general claim that teens are aloof.
reinterpretation: Three precise behaviours that fit both perfectly.
whyItWorks: Comparison proven by a rule of three with parallel grammar. The final "never" breaks the rhythm by being one word.

setup: I'm a big believer in waking up at 5am.
punchline: I just believe in it from bed.
targetAssumption: A believer practises what they believe.
reinterpretation: Belief without practice: theoretical support only.
whyItWorks: The setup copies the confident voice of productivity gurus, and the punch undercuts it with honesty.

setup: I installed a smart doorbell to keep an eye on my house.
punchline: Now it texts me every time I leave, like a worried mother.
targetAssumption: The camera watches strangers for you.
reinterpretation: The camera keeps an eye on you.
whyItWorks: The watcher becomes the watched, then a comparison tag gives it a familiar character.

setup: My manager wants me to take more initiative.
punchline: So I took Dave's. It was barely used.
targetAssumption: "Take initiative" means show more drive.
reinterpretation: Initiative as an object you can take from a colleague.
whyItWorks: It treats an abstract noun as a physical thing. "Barely used" adds a second dig, at Dave.

setup: My kid asked me why the sky is blue.
punchline: I said it's had a long week.
targetAssumption: A science question with a science answer.
reinterpretation: Blue as in sad. The parent's own mood leaks into the answer.
whyItWorks: It sounds like a dad dodging a hard question, and it quietly reveals the dad's week. Two layers, eight words.

setup: A toddler is basically a tiny drunk boss.
punchline: Falls over, shouts orders and fires you at bedtime.
targetAssumption: A toddler is just a small child.
reinterpretation: Every toddler behaviour mapped onto a nightmare manager.
whyItWorks: Three verbs, each true for both worlds, building to "fires you", which is where the boss metaphor pays off.

setup: Every group chat goes through three stages:
punchline: making plans, changing plans and a photo of someone's lunch.
targetAssumption: The stages end with the plan happening.
reinterpretation: The plan never happens. The chat degrades into lunch photos.
whyItWorks: "Making plans, changing plans" sets a tight pattern through repetition, so the third item's break is obvious and fast.

setup: My dad is so cheap, he reuses tea bags
punchline: until it's legally just hot water.
targetAssumption: He reuses them once or twice.
reinterpretation: He reuses them past the point of being tea at all.
whyItWorks: "Legally" brings in official language, which makes the absurd degree sound measured.

setup: Small talk at a party is like a job interview
punchline: where neither of you wants the job.
targetAssumption: It's awkward like an interview.
reinterpretation: Both sides are performing for something neither of them wants.
whyItWorks: The comparison is extended one step further than expected. That extra step ("neither of you wants it") is the real observation.

setup: My mum says I can do anything I put my mind to.
punchline: So I put my mind to a nap.
targetAssumption: An inspiring sentence leading to an achievement.
reinterpretation: "Anything" includes the smallest possible ambition.
whyItWorks: The setup quotes encouragement, the punch shrinks the ambition to its minimum. One syllable punch word.

setup: My flatmate asked me to keep an eye on her soup.
punchline: It burned, but I watched every second.
targetAssumption: "Keep an eye on" means look after.
reinterpretation: Only look at it, and do nothing else.
whyItWorks: Obeys the words, disobeys the meaning. The defensive tone ("but I watched") is a character trait in one line.

setup: My parents told me never to talk to strangers.
punchline: Now they comment on every stranger's Facebook post.
targetAssumption: The rule-givers follow their own rule.
reinterpretation: The rule-givers are now the most strangers-chatty people online.
whyItWorks: Uses their exact rule against them. Repeating "stranger" makes the reversal audible.

setup: Hotel rooms are weird. There's always one light switch that doesn't control anything.
punchline: I think it turns on a light in someone else's room.
targetAssumption: A complaint about bad design.
reinterpretation: It controls something, just not in your room. It's a mystery with a victim.
whyItWorks: Observational comedy: name something everyone has noticed (attitude: weird), then offer an absurd but logical explanation.

setup: Last week I bought a self-cleaning oven. It has never once cleaned itself. Anyway, I asked my teenager to tidy his room and he said he's on it.
punchline: Turns out he's also self-cleaning.
targetAssumption: The oven story is over. We've moved on to a new topic.
reinterpretation: The teenager is another appliance that claims to clean itself and never does.
whyItWorks: A callback rewards the audience for remembering. The earlier line was a joke on its own; now it gains a second target. In a set, the gap between the two would be longer.

setup: My sister is planning her wedding like a military operation.
punchline: The bridesmaids have ranks.
targetAssumption: "Military operation" is a figure of speech for organised.
reinterpretation: It is literally run like an army.
whyItWorks: The punch makes the comparison concrete with one detail. Four words, with the noun last.

setup: My partner and I agreed to split the chores fifty-fifty.
punchline: I do the chores, they do the agreeing.
targetAssumption: Fifty-fifty means each does half the chores.
reinterpretation: The split is between doing chores and agreeing to them.
whyItWorks: Reuses the setup's own word ("agreed") as the punch word, so the audience hears the trick.

setup: My doctor said I need to get out more.
punchline: So I've started sleeping in the garden.
targetAssumption: "Get out more" means socialise.
reinterpretation: Physically be outside, which is technically achieved.
whyItWorks: A gentle literal joke with a sweetly absurd image. It shows the speaker is a little lonely without saying so.

setup: My mum has three love languages:
punchline: food, worry and forwarding me news stories about burglaries.
targetAssumption: Love languages are warm things like gifts and time.
reinterpretation: The third is anxiety dressed up as affection.
whyItWorks: Everyone has this mum. The third item is longer and oddly specific, which makes it feel observed rather than invented.

setup: My bank account is like a goldfish.
punchline: Every month it forgets it ever had anything.
targetAssumption: A goldfish comparison means small.
reinterpretation: The shared quality is memory: money in, and it's gone a moment later.
whyItWorks: Picks the less obvious quality of the comparison object (memory, not size). That small surprise is the laugh.

setup: Car alarms are stupid. When one goes off, nobody thinks "theft".
punchline: Everyone thinks "Steve's sat on his keys."
targetAssumption: The alarm's purpose is to signal a crime.
reinterpretation: It only ever signals Steve.
whyItWorks: Attitude (stupid), then the real, shared reaction. Naming a specific neighbour makes it a scene.

setup: If my nan ran airport security:
punchline: "No liquids, love. But take a sandwich for the flight."
targetAssumption: Security would be strict.
reinterpretation: Security run by nan values feeding you over safety.
whyItWorks: Two strong worlds (security rules, grandmother kindness) collide in her voice. "Love" is the character detail.

setup: I'm not shy. I'm just saving my one good line for the right moment.
punchline: Which was in 2017.
targetAssumption: The right moment is still coming.
reinterpretation: The moment came and went years ago.
whyItWorks: Ending on a specific past date turns hope into regret in one word. Great material for a quiet person: own it before anyone else can.
